prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing atomic clocks to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I opened with circuit QED (B039) at rank 1, but on reflection I no longer think I should be its main advocate. Optical lattice clocks (B015) are the candidate on which the most colleagues independently converge: six of the eight ballots place it in the top four, and the arguments are scientific, not merely popular. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the trap-induced light shift while keeping the Lamb-Dicke regime and many-atom averaging, which is a clear conceptual step. Ye's group then turned it into the record-accuracy and stability instrument, with comparisons across laboratories (JILA, RIKEN, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) agreeing near 10^-18. The consequences are concrete and checkable: tests of fundamental constants and of relativistic effects through geodesy, and the roadmap to a redefinition of the second. The two-name credit follows the proposal-plus-realisation split cleanly, and the result is mature, reproduced and stable in interpretation.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision timekeeping has already been recognised along an unbroken line: Hall and Haensch (frequency combs, 2005) and Wineland (single-ion clocks and quantum control, 2012) cover much of the enabling technology, so a committee could say the lattice clock is a refinement of a rewarded programme. The formal redefinition of the second has not yet happened, which some will read as the application milestone still lying ahead. Credit also sits uneasily with a two-name cap, since the Ye-group clock work builds on contributions from many co-workers (for example Ludlow, Bloom, Lemke, Hinkley) and on the comb and ultrastable-laser infrastructure, and Katori's early Sr work and Ye's record-performance work are not the same kind of contribution.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B015 first as a compact, fair two-name credit that continues the long Nobel line from precision spectroscopy, with 1e-18 performance confirmed by several laboratories.
responses.response: I agree on the core and have moved it from my fifth place to my first. Where I qualify his view is the Nobel-line argument: continuity with Hall, Haensch and Wineland is exactly the point a sceptic will raise, so the citation should be worded around the magic-wavelength lattice concept and its realisation, not generic clock accuracy. I accept his judgement that two names are enough, but the committee should say plainly why Ye is credited for the performance frontier and not only for a refinement.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the IceCube neutrino discovery first as a clear, nameable discovery of nature and puts circuit QED second, but notes that the recent prize for circuit-based macroscopic quantum effects may make a distinct circuit-QED recognition hard to defend.
responses.response: His second point is fair, and it is the main reason I step back from my own rank 1. Circuit QED (photon-coupled artificial atoms, dispersive readout) is physically distinct from macroscopic tunnelling and energy quantisation, but a committee will be reluctant to return to superconducting circuits so soon, and I am too close to the field to argue that confidently. On B014 I respect the discovery-of-nature argument and the maturity of the diffuse-flux confirmation; my reservation is that credit in a large-collaboration result is hard to place on two names, which he acknowledges. I would keep B014 as a serious candidate for a later year but I do not rank it above B015 now.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks topological insulators (B018 with Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan) second as a coherent theory-to-observation narrative with very high originality, and fluctuation theorems (B005) first.
responses.response: I share his view that B018 is a deep and mature concept and I ranked it fourth. My qualification is attribution: the shortlist itself carries two different trios (B018 with Hasan, B003 with Xue) and the foundational Kane-Mele paper has Mele as co-author, who is not in the three-name set, so the allocation is much less settled than for B015. On B005 I cannot match his enthusiasm in his own field of statistical physics, but I note it has only one ranking in the opening, so I leave that judgement to those who know the area.

responses.point: Pearce places trapped-ion computation (B009) fourth but warns that part of it may be covered by the 2012 prize and that 2025 recognised superconducting circuits.
responses.response: I agree and it changed how I weigh the quantum-computing candidates: B009 was my rank 2, and I now think the 2012 and 2025 prizes together narrow the novelty for both trapped ions and circuit QED. His own rank 3 for B015 is consistent with my move, and I would add that B015 has not been touched by either of those two citations in the way the quantum-computing candidates have.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 precision-measurement prizes.
Whether two names fairly represent the experimental credit for the 10^-18 clocks, given the many contributors in the Ye group and elsewhere.
Whether recognition should wait for the redefinition of the second.
My own ranking of circuit QED could be biased by my closeness to the field, and I cannot judge fully how the 2025 prize shapes its prospects.
statement.conflict_note: My profile documents connections that may require recusal on B039 (circuit QED) and nearby superconducting-circuit candidates: I direct WACQT at Chalmers, I succeeded Per Delsing in that role, and Chalmers colleagues (Delsing, C. M. Wilson) and frequent co-author Anton Frisk Kockum work in superconducting circuits and waveguide QED, and I presented the 2025 prize. No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B015, the preferred configuration.
